**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Here is a skill that shows up on every test you will ever take, and in every article you will ever read: figuring out what a text is *really* about.

1. Read **The Suitcase Test** — it gives you a trick you can use forever.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble** and the **Crossword**.
3. Keep the **Main Idea Moves** chart open while you work.
4. Practice on **Which Detail Does Not Belong?**
5. Take the quiz — it uses short paragraphs, so read each one twice.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your own main-idea statements.
7. Read **Reading Questions** if you are wondering how this works on videos, or what to do when you disagree with an author.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Suitcase Test** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Main-Idea Poster for Younger Readers** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Watch out for the most common trap: the topic is not the main idea. "Dogs" is a topic. "Dogs can be trained to detect illness" is a main idea. 🧳

from:
## The Suitcase Test

Imagine you are packing a suitcase for a trip. The suitcase is the **main idea** — the one big container. The clothes you pack inside are the **supporting details**. Everything that goes in has to belong to that trip.

When you read a paragraph, you are doing the same job in reverse. You look at what is packed and figure out what suitcase it all came from.

Here is a paragraph:

> Honeybees do far more than make honey. As they move from flower to flower, pollen sticks to their bodies and travels with them, which lets plants make seeds. About one out of every three bites of food people eat depends on a pollinator like a bee. Farmers of almonds, apples, and blueberries even rent beehives during flowering season.

What is it about? A first instinct is "bees" — but that is only the **topic**, the one-word subject. The main idea is a full thought: *honeybees are important to our food supply because they pollinate crops.*

That is the difference students miss most. The topic is a word. The main idea is a sentence that says something ABOUT the topic.

Notice how the details worked. Pollen sticking to bees, one in three bites, farmers renting hives — each one supports the same claim. That is your test: if a sentence does not help prove the main idea, it does not belong in that suitcase.

Sometimes the main idea is stated right in the text, often in the first or last sentence. That is the easy version. Other times it is **implied** — never written down anywhere, and you have to build it yourself from the details. Both count. Both are findable.

A quick method that works: read the whole paragraph, then cover it and ask yourself, "If I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?" Whatever you say out loud is usually very close to the main idea.

One warning. A detail can be true, interesting, and still not be the main idea. "Bees have five eyes" is a fact, and it is fascinating, but a paragraph about pollination is not really about bee eyes. Interesting and important are different things — and telling them apart is most of what good reading is.

## The Suitcase Test

Imagine you are packing a suitcase for a trip. The suitcase is the **main idea** — the one big container. The clothes you pack inside are the **supporting details**. Everything that goes in has to belong to that trip.

When you read a paragraph, you are doing the same job in reverse. You look at what is packed and figure out what suitcase it all came from.

Here is a paragraph:

> Honeybees do far more than make honey. As they move from flower to flower, pollen sticks to their bodies and travels with them, which lets plants make seeds. Many fruit and nut crops benefit from insect pollination. Farmers of almonds, apples, and blueberries even rent beehives during flowering season.

What is it about? A first instinct is "bees" — but that is only the **topic**, the one-word subject. The main idea is a full thought: *honeybees are important to our food supply because they pollinate crops.*

That is the difference students miss most. The topic can be a word or short phrase. The main idea is a sentence that says something ABOUT the topic.

Notice how the details worked. Pollen sticking to bees, food crops benefiting from pollination, farmers renting hives — each one supports the same claim. That is your test: if a detail does not support the main idea, it may be background or less relevant to this particular point.

Sometimes the main idea is stated right in the text, often in the first or last sentence. That is the easy version. Other times it is **implied** — never written down anywhere, and you have to build it yourself from the details. Both count. Both are findable.

A quick method that works: read the whole paragraph, then cover it and ask yourself, "If I could only say one sentence about this, what would it be?" Treat that sentence as a first draft, then check it against the important details.

One warning. A detail can be true, interesting, and still not be the main idea. "Bees have five eyes" is a fact, and it is fascinating, but a paragraph about pollination is not really about bee eyes. Interesting and important are different things — and telling them apart is most of what good reading is.

The suitcase is an analogy. Real paragraphs can include examples, qualifications and background. Focus on the important information, and allow more than one accurate wording of a main idea. You may keep the text visible, annotate, write or use AAC instead of covering it and speaking.

from: Supports: 'Bees matter to our food supply'

from: True, but does NOT support that idea
to: Other bee facts

from: About one in three bites of our food depends on pollinators
to: Many fruit and nut crops benefit from bee pollination

from: A bee's wings beat over 200 times per second
to: Honey bees have six legs

to: Honey bees build wax comb

to: Bee visits help blueberry flowers produce fruit

from: You picked a main idea, but one detail in the paragraph does not support it. What does that most likely mean?
to: You picked a main idea, but an important detail does not fit. What is the best next step?

from: Read: 'Some hospitals now keep therapy dogs on staff. Patients who spend time with them report less pain and lower stress. Nurses say children agree to difficult procedures more easily when a dog is present.' Write the main idea in one sentence.
to: Read this invented classroom example: 'The library opened a quiet corner. It added soft seats, dimmer lamps and sound-absorbing panels. Readers now have a place away from the busy entrance.' Write the main idea in one sentence.

from: Therapy dogs help patients in hospitals by reducing pain and stress and making difficult procedures easier — especially for children.
to: The library created a quieter, more comfortable place to read. Accept an equivalent statement that covers the changes and their purpose.

from: A single paragraph usually has one. Whole articles often have several, one per section. Handling that is exactly what the 5th grade standard asks of you.
to: A paragraph often develops one main point, but structure varies. Longer texts may develop several related ideas. Choose a statement that fits the section you are summarizing.

from: Because it sits underneath almost every other reading skill. If you can find what a text is really about, you can answer most questions about it.
to: Finding the main idea helps connect details and understand a text. Other reading tasks may also require vocabulary, inference, comparison or evaluating evidence.

from: Exactly the same. Ask what one sentence captures the whole thing. The suitcase test does not care what form the ideas arrive in.
to: Yes, the same questions can help with videos and podcasts. Pause, replay or use a transcript when helpful, and consider sound and visual information too.

from: The topic is a word; the main idea is a sentence that says something about the topic.
to: The topic is a word or phrase; the main idea is a sentence that says something about the topic.
